question: Who counts as a heretic, and what makes someone one?

answers.label: One who chooses his own teaching against the faith received from the apostles
Error becomes heresy when held obstinately after correction

overview.text: "Heresy" means choice. Ignatius calls it a foreign plant mixed with Christ like poison in honeyed wine; Tertullian defines the heretic as one who chooses his own teaching instead of what the apostles handed on.

Irenaeus adds the test of publicity: error never shows itself bare, but dressed to seem truer than truth, and its teachers, when appealed to the apostolic tradition kept through the succession of presbyters, claim to be wiser than the apostles themselves.
Augustine added that a mistaken person is not yet a heretic: he becomes one when, warned, he defends his error obstinately.

quotes.author: Ignatius of Antioch
quotes.english: I urge you, then, not I but the love of Jesus Christ: use only Christian food, and keep away from a foreign plant, which is heresy. These people mix Jesus Christ with themselves to gain trust, like those who give a deadly drug with honeyed wine, which the unknowing take gladly, with evil pleasure, to their death.
quotes.original: Παρακαλῶ οὖν ὑμᾶς, οὐκ ἐγώ, ἀλλ’ ἡ ἀγάπη Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ: μόνῃ τῇ χριστιανῇ τροφῇ χρῆσθε, ἀλλοτρίας δὲ βοτάνης ἀπέχεσθε, ἥτις ἐστὶν αἵρεσις: οἳ ἑαυτοῖς παρεμπλέκουσιν Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν καταξιοπιστευόμενοι, ὥσπερ θανάσιμον φάρμακον διδόντες μετὰ οἰνομέλιτος, ὅπερ ὁ ἀγνοῶν ἡδέως λαμβάνει ἐν ἡδονῇ κακῇ τὸ ἀ
quotes.context: The heresy Ignatius has in mind is the denial of Christ's real flesh.

quotes.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
quotes.english: For error by itself is not put on show, lest once stripped bare it be exposed; but decked out cunningly in a plausible garment, it makes itself seem, by its outward appearance, even truer than the truth itself to the inexperienced.
quotes.original: ἡ γὰρ πλάνη καθ᾽ αὑτὴν μὲν οὐκ ἐπιδείκνυται, ἵνα μὴ γυμνωθεῖσα γένηται κατάφωρος· πιθανῷ δὲ περιβλήματι πανούργως κοσμουμένη, καὶ αὐτῆς τῆς ἀληθείας ἀληθεστέραν ἑαυτὴν παρέχει φαίνεσθαι διὰ τῆς ἔξωθεν φαντασίας τοῖς ἀπειροτέροις
quotes.context: The preface to the whole work. The heretical teaching persuades because it is dressed to look like truth; Irenaeus says it must therefore be stripped and shown false, not merely denounced. The Greek of the preface is preserved in the PG 7 text.

quotes.author: Irenaeus of Lyons
quotes.english: Yet when we appeal to them with that tradition again, the one from the apostles, which is preserved in the churches through the successions of the presbyters, they oppose the tradition, claiming that they, wiser not only than the presbyters but also than the apostles, have found the unmixed truth.
quotes.original: Cum autem ad eam iterum traditionem, quae est ab Apostolis, quae per successiones Presbyterorum in Ecclesiis custoditur, provocamus eos, adversantur traditioni, dicentes se non solum Presbyteris, sed etiam Apostolis exsistentes sapientiores, sinceram invenisse veritatem
quotes.context: For Irenaeus the mark of the heretic is a rival, self found truth set against the public apostolic tradition. He adds that anyone can inspect that tradition in every church and count the bishops the apostles appointed (3.3), and that the truth is therefore not to be sought elsewhere (3.4). The Greek of Book 3 is lost here; the passage survives in the Latin translation.

quotes.author: Tertullian
quotes.english: Heresies are so called from the Greek word for choice, which a person uses either to found them or to take them up. That is why the apostle called the heretic self-condemned, for he has chosen for himself that in which he is condemned. But we may not indulge in anything of our own will, nor choose what someone else has brought in of his own will. We have the apostles of the Lord as our authorities, who did not themselves choose to bring in anything of their own will, but faithfully delivered to the nations the teaching received from Christ.
quotes.original: haereses dictae Graeca voce, ex interpretatione electionis qua quis sive ad instituendas sive ad suscipiendas eas utitur. Ideo et sibi damnatum dixit haereticum, quia et in quo damnatur sibi elegit. Nobis vere nihil ex nostro arbitrio indulgere licet, sed nec eligere quod aliquis de arbitrio suo induxerit. Apostolos domini habemus auctores, qui nec ipsi quicquam ex suo arbitrio quod inducerent elegerunt, sed acceptam a Christo disciplinam fideliter nationibus assignaverunt.
quotes.context: "Hairesis" means choice. The heretic chooses his own teaching instead of receiving the apostles'.

quotes.author: Augustine of Hippo
quotes.english: It makes a difference how much, and from what source, and finally whether, when warned, a person corrects himself or, by defending it obstinately, turns into dogma what he had said lightly and not as dogma. So since every heretic is also a fool, but not every fool is at once to be called a heretic ...
quotes.original: sed interest quanto, interest unde, interest postremo utrum admonitus corrigat an pertinaciter defendendo etiam dogma faciat, quod leuitate, non dogmate dixerat. cum igitur omnis haereticus consequenter et stultus sit, non autem omnis stultus continuo sit appellandus haereticus
quotes.context: Error becomes heresy when it is held obstinately after correction. Augustine says the same in City of God 18.51.

quotes.author: Vincent of Lérins
quotes.english: In the Catholic Church itself, the greatest care must be taken that we hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. ... what the very force of the name and its meaning declares, taking in, as it does, nearly all things together.
quotes.original: In ipsa item catholica ecclesia magnopere curandum est ut id teneamus quod ubique, quod semper, quod ab omnibus creditum est ... quod ipsa vis nominis ratioque declarat, quae omnia fere universaliter comprehendit
quotes.context: Vincent's canon, written about 434, three years after the Council of Ephesus: a teaching is unmasked as a private choice when it fails the triple test of universality, antiquity, and consent. It became the classic rule for telling the faith the Church received from what a teacher invents.

source.edition: Moxon, The Commonitorium of Vincent of Lerins (Cambridge, 1915)

quotes.author: Thomas Aquinas
quotes.english: because he does not choose the things truly handed down by Christ, but the things his own mind suggests to him. ... And so heresy is a species of unbelief, belonging to those who profess the faith of Christ but corrupt its dogmas.
quotes.original: quia non eligit ea quae sunt vere a Christo tradita, sed ea quae sibi propria mens suggerit. ... Et ideo haeresis est infidelitatis species pertinens ad eos qui fidem Christi profitentur, sed eius dogmata corrumpunt.
quotes.context: Thomas builds the definition from the word itself: heresy (haeresis) is a choosing. The heretic means to assent to Christ, but picks what to believe by his own mind instead of what Christ handed down; unbelief of that kind, in someone who professes the faith of Christ, is heresy.

source.edition: Summa Theologiae, Latin text (Leonine), via Documenta Catholica Omnia
